topics.topic: Atomic request admission and last-request update relative to session expiry
questions: What happens when a request passes the arrival-time session check but, before it acquires the session lock or records its arrival, the expiry pass acquires that lock and ends the session?
What event defines a request's arrival, and how is last_request updated atomically for ordinary and concurrent requests without violating the stated locking behavior?

How is an ordinary owner request’s validity check and update of last_request made atomic with the expiry pass, so the pass cannot expire the session using the previous last_request after a valid request has arrived?

What happens when a request passes the session check, then the expiry pass acquires the locks and removes that session before the request acquires the session lock or uses its pending confirmation or uploaded file?

judgement.why: This is the same question about atomic arrival-time validity, last-request renewal and expiry ordering already judged in P6, and the relevant passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Atomic last-request-time updates and their ordering against expiry
quotes:
An owner
   request is any request to the owner interface that
   carries the valid session, whatever its answer; its arrival restarts the 30
   minutes — of concurrent requests the latest arrival counts; before the
   first request it runs from the sign-in.

Validity is
   checked when a request arrives (A04 rule 6, stage 1); a request that
   passes it completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs, and
   a restart that interrupts it leaves nothing of it (A04 rule 4).
precedent.why: Validity and idle renewal are explicitly decided at request arrival, so a request arriving before the limit remains admitted even if a sweep later obtains the lock.

topics.topic: Backup cryptographic format, key handling, key digest, and metadata authentication
questions: What exact authenticated-encryption format and key-handling rules must every release use to create and verify a backup?

Is the unencrypted record merely parseable and trusted as read, or must its values be authenticated against the ciphertext before they control listing, retention, deletion, restore-key selection, and the recorded sequence check?
Which authenticated-encryption construction and key handling are required, and are the unencrypted metadata and ciphertext authenticated together so either cannot be altered undetected?
How is the key digest computed and represented, and is it merely a key identifier or a security check that must be collision-resistant and authenticated?

What fixed cryptographic format must every implementation use, including authenticated encryption, nonce generation, treatment of backup keys longer than an algorithm key, the key-digest algorithm, and authentication of the readable metadata?

judgement.why: This is the same question about backup encryption, authentication, key digest, nonce handling and metadata binding already judged in P12, and the relevant passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Backup encryption, authentication, key digest, nonce, and metadata binding
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Expiry-pass cadence, missed-pass handling, scope, and locking
questions: If a pass is still running or blocked when another 60-second boundary arrives, are missed passes queued, skipped, coalesced into one pass, or does completion shift the cadence?

If a pass is delayed, lasts longer than 60 seconds, or the host resumes after several intervals, are missed passes skipped, coalesced or run repeatedly; which sessions belong to a pass; and is the import lock held for the whole pass or acquired separately for each session?
After suspension or a pass lasting beyond its next scheduled tick, does Registry run one pass immediately, run every missed pass, or schedule the next pass 60 seconds after resumption or completion?

judgement.why: This is the same question about expiry-pass cadence, missed passes, overrun behavior and lock scope already judged in P15, and the relevant passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Expiry-pass initial timing, recurring schedule, missed passes, and lock scope
quotes:
Registry
   ends it — and drops its pending confirmation and its uploaded file with it
   (M11) — at a pass over the sessions it makes every 60 seconds from the
   start; the pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import
   lock and then each session's lock (A16 rule 2) and deciding under them.

A session that has reached a limit serves no request from that
   moment: a request carrying it is refused at the session check.
precedent.why: The limits themselves determine request refusal exactly, so the first tick, delayed-tick policy and overlap handling affect only internal reclamation of already inaccessible session state.

topics.topic: Daily backup eligibility after missed 03:00 checks or overlapping runs
questions: If the clock moves forward from before 03:00 to after 03:00 within the same UTC date, does that date run because the earlier look saw the same date, or is every forward jump past 03:00 treated as a missed run?
After the preceding run finishes later that day, may a later clock look start the skipped date's run, or is that date permanently marked as missed?

quotes:
a date's
   run starts at its first look at or after 03:00 of that date when an
   earlier look of the same process saw that date before 03:00, and no kept
   backup of that date exists

A clock set forward past 03:00 of a date gives that date no
   run, the earlier look having seen another date, and the dates jumped over
   get none either.

Runs
   never overlap: a 03:00 that finds a run still going makes no run of its
   own.
judgement.why: A forward move past 03:00 within the same date satisfies the same-date earlier-look rule, whereas the stated no-run case requires the earlier look to have seen another date; an overlapping run makes the date miss its run rather than retry later.

topics.topic: OwnerSession monotonic timing state and wall-clock expiry meaning
questions: What timing facts does M11 actually store and use so that its UTC instants and stated expiry remain consistent with authoritative monotonic deadlines after the wall clock changes?
What monotonic values does M11 retain to enforce session, idle and confirmation limits after wall-clock changes, and what does its wall-clock “expiry at the latest” mean then?

quotes: Every time Registry records is an instant in UTC with time zone (L16).

Facts: its identity, minted by Registry at sign-in ("Identity formats");
written once: the instant it began, its expiry at the latest and its CSRF
value (R0-29); changed by the owner's requests (State 2 A13, A16; owner,
2026-10-31): the instant of its last request, which starts as the instant it
began; at most one pending confirmation — its one-time value, the action, its
target, the revision or access version and the inputs it is bound to, and
the instant it was shown — made when a confirmation step is shown, replaced
by the next one shown and cleared when used; and at most one uploaded import
file, replaced by the next upload and dropped when the import is accepted.

Every duration in this decision — the 8 hours, the 30, 15 and 10
   minutes, the 60 seconds — is measured by the process's monotonic clock,
   which a change of the wall clock does not move and which counts the time
   the host or its VM was suspended, so a session does not outlive a
   suspension; instants Registry records
   and the 03:00 of A18 are UTC wall-clock time.
judgement.divergence: One implementer can enforce expiry from the recorded UTC instants, causing a forward or backward wall-clock change to shorten or extend validity; another can retain additional monotonic deadlines and use the UTC instants only as descriptive values, preserving the stated durations. The owner notices whether the session or confirmation remains usable after a wall-clock change.
judgement.why: The texts require monotonic enforcement and exhaustively describe the session's recorded UTC facts, but do not say what monotonic state is retained or how the recorded latest-expiry instant relates to the authoritative monotonic deadline.

topics.topic: Backup filename prefixes, timestamp encoding, precision, and collision handling
questions: What exact prefixes and filename encoding must every release use, including precision and collision behavior for equal recorded instants?

topics.topic: Durable backup commit point and required file-system synchronization
questions: When is a backup durably considered kept, and what file and directory synchronisation is required so a crash cannot leave a kept name containing incomplete data or lose a backup already reported as kept?

topics.topic: Retention-age measurement and bounds across wall-clock changes
questions: Does the 30-day and at-most-31-day guarantee measure elapsed time despite wall-clock changes, or UTC timestamp difference; and what bound applies if the wall clock is moved backward or forward?

topics.topic: Whether session expiry immediately deletes temporary data or waits for cleanup
questions: At a time limit, does the session and its temporary data end immediately, or does it merely become invalid and remain stored until the next cleanup pass?
